questions.explain: Conversations are durable, append-mostly history; sessions are ephemeral, read-modify-write coordination state with a TTL — opposite access patterns, so they are modeled separately.
options: They are the same thing with different names
Sessions are durable and conversations expire
Sessions are ephemeral coordination state with a TTL; conversations are durable history
Sessions live in Redis and conversations in SQL Server by requirement
questions.q: What is the distinction between a session and a conversation?

questions.explain: sp_getapplock on the session ID with Exclusive mode and Session ownership serializes turns across all API instances; the lock auto-releases when the connection closes, so crashes leave no orphaned locks.
options: sp_getapplock on the session ID (Exclusive, Session owner) — a database-level named lock that auto-releases on connection close
An application-level mutex in each API instance
A CHECK constraint on the sessions table
Row-level locking with READPAST
questions.q: How does the chapter prevent two API instances from interleaving generations for the same session?

questions.explain: The expiry job UPDATEs sessions to 'closed' with OUTPUT ... INTO dbo.session_close_queue, atomically closing sessions and enqueueing summarization work in one statement.
options: A polling loop that deletes expired rows
A SQL Agent job that emails an admin
UPDATE to 'closed' with OUTPUT ... INTO the close queue — atomic close plus enqueue in one statement
Truncating the sessions table nightly
questions.q: How does session expiry trigger follow-up work like summarization?

questions.explain: In-flight sessions keep their prompt version (system_prompt_version) because mid-conversation prompt swaps produce incoherent behavior and invalidate prompt-version comparisons in evaluation.
options: Prompts are stored only in application config
In-flight sessions are pinned to their prompt version; new sessions pick up the current version
All sessions immediately switch to the newest prompt
Prompt versions are never tracked
questions.q: How does the chapter handle prompt versioning for long-lived sessions?

questions.explain: No sticky sessions are needed — lock, state, and history all live in SQL Server so any instance can serve any session; expiry must be computed in T-SQL with SYSUTCDATETIME() because the database clock is the single source of truth.
options: Use sticky sessions so each user stays on one instance
Store session state in each API instance's memory
Compare expiry in application code using the instance clock
Keep instances stateless with all coordination in SQL Server, and compute expiry with SYSUTCDATETIME()
questions.q: How do multiple API instances coordinate without sticky sessions, and what clock rule applies?
